analogy.p: Imagine a family building a sandcastle on a beach as the tide comes in. A wall of stones around it is like hard engineering: strong but costly and it changes the beach. Piling extra sand on the seaward side is like beach nourishment: it needs topping up every tide. Moving the castle further up the beach is like managed retreat: it gives up some ground but is the cheapest in the long run. The analogy works because every option trades cost against protection. It breaks down because a real coast has people, property and wildlife with competing needs, and the sea level is rising.

bullets: **Hard engineering:** artificial structures built to resist the sea (sea walls, rock armour, groynes, gabions).
**Soft engineering:** working with natural processes (beach nourishment, dune regeneration).
**Managed retreat / realignment:** allowing the sea to flood or erode land in a controlled way.
**Case study:** one named UK scheme with reasons, strategy, effects and conflicts.
You must be able to **justify** a strategy for a given place and **evaluate** its costs and benefits.
Command words: **describe**, **explain**, **assess**, **evaluate**, **to what extent**.
Always link strategy to the **process it is designed to stop**: wave attack, longshore drift, mass movement or flooding.
**Link to other topics:** processes and landforms in geo.2.1 and geo.2.2; sea level rise and climate change in the hazards topics.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA wants you to know the **management strategies** used on coasts and an **example of a coastal management scheme in the UK**. For the strategies you must be able to describe how each works and give its advantages, disadvantages and costs. The categories are **hard engineering** (sea walls, rock armour, groynes, gabions), **soft engineering** (beach nourishment, dune regeneration) and **managed retreat** (coastal realignment, and in some plans 'do nothing'). For the example you must give the **reasons for management, the management strategy, and the resulting effects and conflicts**. The main skill is evaluation: no strategy is perfect, and choices depend on cost, benefit, effect on other areas and sustainability.

bullets: **Risks:** coastal erosion, coastal flooding (storm surges), landslides and rock falls.
**What is at risk:** homes, roads, railways, farmland, power stations, historic sites, tourism infrastructure.
**Economic value:** protecting a town of thousands of people is easier to justify than protecting a few farm fields.
**Social impacts:** loss of homes, blight (property that cannot be sold) and stress for residents.
**Environmental value:** habitats such as salt marsh, dunes and sand flats are protected by law (SSSIs, special protection areas).
Management can be **local** (a council defending a seafront) or **national** (strategy set by the Environment Agency and Defra).
**Natural causes** such as soft rock, strong waves and a long fetch make some sections more vulnerable.
**Human actions** such as building defences, dredging and sand extraction can increase erosion elsewhere.
core.p: Coasts need to be managed because they are **dynamic** (they keep changing) and because many people live, work and play there. Erosion removes land, undermining roads and homes; flooding threatens low-lying land and settlements; and landslides on soft cliffs can destroy property. At the same time coasts are valuable for **tourism, ports, industry, farming and wildlife**. The decision to protect or not depends on the value of what is at risk compared with the cost of protection. Sea level rise and more frequent storms linked to climate change are increasing the pressure, so the demand for management will rise.

bullets: **How it works:** a strong barrier that reflects wave energy; the curved lip sends waves back to sea.
**Advantages:** very effective; long life (often 50 or more years); gives a promenade for visitors; protects expensive property.
**Disadvantages:** very high cost to build and maintain (thousands of pounds per metre); can look unnatural.
**Beach scour:** reflected waves can erode the beach in front, which may then expose the base of the wall.
**Sediment starvation:** stopping cliff erosion reduces the supply of material to beaches elsewhere.
**Best used** to protect high-value areas such as towns and ports where the cost is justified.
**Example use:** many seaside resorts such as Blackpool, Brighton and Lyme Regis have sea walls.
**Evaluation tip:** link effectiveness to cost; say what the benefits to people are, and who pays.
core.p: A **sea wall** is a concrete or stone barrier built at the foot of a cliff or at the back of a beach, often with a **curved or recurved face** which reflects wave energy back out to sea and stops waves from overtopping. Sea walls give a high level of protection and last for decades. They also provide a promenade and may support roads or buildings. However, they are very **expensive** to build and maintain, and they can look ugly. Waves reflected from the wall can scour away the beach in front of it, so the beach level drops and the wall may be undermined. The wall also stops natural erosion of the cliff, so sediment supply to beaches down the coast is reduced.

bullets: **Rock armour:** boulders (often granite or limestone) piled against the cliff or wall; waves break on them and lose energy.
**Rock armour advantages:** cheaper than a sea wall; easy to maintain; provides habitats in the gaps; flexible and can be rearranged.
**Rock armour disadvantages:** expensive to transport; may look ugly; can be hazardous to walk on; may be moved by large storms.
**Gabions:** wire cages filled with rocks; cheap, quick and often used to stabilise cliff slopes or small stretches.
**Gabion disadvantages:** short life, the wire rusts and breaks; ugly; limited strength.
Both **absorb** rather than reflect wave energy, so there is less scour than with a smooth wall.
Rock armour needs **regular repair** as boulders settle and shift.
**Example use:** Mappleton (Holderness) used rock armour and groynes to protect the village.
core.h: Hard engineering: rock armour and gabions
core.p: **Rock armour** (also called riprap) is a pile of large boulders placed at the foot of a cliff or in front of a sea wall. The gaps between the boulders force waves to break and absorb their energy, so the cliff or defence behind is protected. It is cheaper and easier to build than a sea wall, and can be added to existing defences. It needs the rock to be **brought from elsewhere**, often from Scandinavia, which adds cost and carbon emissions, and it can look unattractive and make access to the beach difficult. **Gabions** are wire cages filled with small rocks, stacked at the base of a cliff or on a slope. They are cheap and flexible but have a short life as the wire corrodes and the cages can break, so they are used to protect low-value land.

bullets: **How it works:** groynes interrupt longshore drift so sand and shingle are deposited against them.
**Advantages:** relatively cheap; keep a beach for tourism; the beach itself is a natural defence.
**Disadvantages:** starve the beach downdrift, causing more erosion there; can look ugly; timber needs maintenance.
**Spacing and length** matter: if too long or too close, they cut off too much sediment.
Often used **together with beach nourishment** so that the fresh sand stays in place.
**Updrift** is the direction the sediment comes from; **downdrift** is where it is travelling to.
**Example:** at Mappleton, two rock groynes protected the village but increased erosion at the next section of coast to the south.
**Evaluation tip:** a good answer says who benefits and who loses.
core.p: **Groynes** are timber or rock barriers built at right angles to the beach, from the top of the beach down towards the sea. They **trap sediment** moved by longshore drift, so a wider beach builds up on the updrift side. The wider beach absorbs wave energy and protects the coast behind, and also gives more space for tourists. They are relatively cheap and widely used. The problem is **downdrift**: because the groynes trap sand, the beach further along the coast is starved of sediment, so it becomes narrower and the cliff behind erodes faster. This can cause conflict between neighbouring communities, and groynes do nothing to stop erosion by storm waves that overtop them.

bullets: **Beach nourishment:** sand or shingle added to the beach; absorbs wave energy; usually cheaper than hard engineering.
**Nourishment advantages:** natural appearance; benefits tourism; no harm to other areas.
**Nourishment disadvantages:** must be repeated (ongoing cost); dredging disturbs marine wildlife; sand may not match the original.
**Dune regeneration:** marram grass planted, fencing, boardwalks to stop trampling; roots bind the sand.
**Dune advantages:** cheap; natural; supports wildlife; absorbs energy.
**Dune disadvantages:** needs management of visitors; takes time to grow; limited protection in severe storms.
Soft engineering is **more sustainable** because it does not need heavy construction and is natural.
**Best for:** areas with a lower value of land, or where natural beaches already exist.
core.h: Soft engineering: beach nourishment and dune regeneration
core.p: **Soft engineering** works with natural processes rather than against them. **Beach nourishment** (replenishment) adds sand or shingle, usually dredged from the sea bed offshore, to a beach that has been eroded. The wider, higher beach absorbs wave energy and protects the land. It looks natural and benefits tourism, and costs less than a sea wall. However, it must be repeated every few years because the sea continues to remove material, so costs continue, and the dredging damages the sea-bed habitat. **Dune regeneration** protects and rebuilds sand dunes by planting marram grass, building fences to trap blown sand, and restricting access by walkers. Dunes absorb wave energy and are a habitat for wildlife.

bullets: **Managed retreat:** deliberately let the sea flood land behind the old line of defence.
**Advantages:** cheap in the long run; creates salt marsh and wildlife habitat; provides natural flood storage; sustainable.
**Disadvantages:** loss of farmland and property; compensation needed; people may oppose; takes time for salt marsh to develop.
**Do nothing / no active intervention:** no money spent; coast erodes naturally; cost to the owners.
**Blight:** homes in areas where defences will no longer be maintained lose value and cannot be sold.
**Example:** Medmerry (West Sussex) created new intertidal habitat and protected properties behind a new inland embankment, completed about 2013.
**Suitable for:** low-value farmland, areas where defence cost is greater than the value protected.
**Evaluation tip:** link to **sustainability**: short-term loss for long-term gain.
core.h: Managed retreat (coastal realignment) and do nothing
core.p: **Managed retreat**, also called **managed realignment**, means allowing the sea to flood or erode areas of low-value land in a controlled way. Existing defences are removed or breached and new defences are built further inland. The newly flooded land develops into **salt marsh** or mudflats, which absorb wave energy and provide a natural defence and wildlife habitat. It is cheaper in the long term and sustainable, but people who lose homes or farmland suffer, and need to be compensated. It can cause conflict as the benefits are for the wider area and the costs are for a few people. **No active intervention** (do nothing) means not building or maintaining any defence. It costs nothing but may cause loss of land and property.

bullets: **Hold the line:** keep defences where they are; used for towns, ports and power stations.
**Advance the line:** build new defences out to sea to reclaim land; very rare and expensive.
**Managed realignment:** move the line of defence inland; sea floods low-value land.
**No active intervention:** let nature take its course; used where costs outweigh benefits.
**Cost-benefit analysis:** benefits (value protected) divided by costs; a ratio above 1 means worth doing.
**Stakeholders** include homeowners, farmers, councils, wildlife groups, tourism businesses and the government.
Funding mostly comes from central government; local people sometimes contribute.
**Conflicts:** between those protected and those whose coast is eroded faster; between conservation and development.
core.h: Shoreline management plans and decision making
core.p: In England and Wales, **Shoreline Management Plans (SMPs)** divide the coast into sections and give each a policy for the next 20, 50 and 100 years. There are four main policy options: **hold the line** (maintain or upgrade defences), **advance the line** (build new defences seaward of the existing line), **managed realignment** (let the shoreline move back in a controlled way) and **no active intervention** (do not maintain or build defences). Decisions are based on a **cost-benefit analysis**: the value of the land, property and infrastructure protected is compared with the cost of the defences. Where the benefits are less than the costs, protection is unlikely to be funded. Local people, councils, the Environment Agency, conservation groups and businesses are consulted, which can lead to conflict.

bullets: **Most costly:** sea walls; **cheaper:** rock armour, groynes, gabions; **cheapest:** do nothing, dune regeneration.
**Longest life:** sea wall (50 or more years); **shortest:** gabions, nourishment (needs repeating).
**Most natural:** soft engineering and managed retreat.
**Most effective in a major storm:** sea wall plus rock armour; least: gabions and dunes.
**Effects elsewhere:** groynes can cause more erosion downdrift; sea walls may reduce sediment supply to beaches.
**Sustainable:** soft engineering and managed retreat; **less sustainable:** large concrete structures.
Combine strategies: e.g. groynes with beach nourishment, rock armour with dune planting.
**Higher-level argument:** it is not 'which is best' but 'which is best here' given the value at risk and available money.
core.h: Comparing strategies: cost, effectiveness and sustainability
core.p: When you compare strategies you should consider **cost** (building and maintaining), **effectiveness** (how well it stops erosion or flooding), **lifespan**, **environmental impact**, **appearance** and **effects on other places**. Hard engineering is generally effective and long lasting but is costly and can harm other areas. Soft engineering costs less and looks more natural but may have to be repeated and gives less protection in a big storm. Managed retreat is the most sustainable but may involve the loss of valuable land. The best coastal management usually uses a **combination**, such as a sea wall in the town and managed realignment on nearby farmland. A strategy is **sustainable** if it meets the needs of people today without damaging the environment or increasing costs for future generations.

bullets: **Location:** Lyme Regis, on the Dorset coast, within the Jurassic Coast World Heritage Site.
**Geology:** weak clays and shales are saturated by rainfall, so slopes slide towards the sea.
**Waves:** strong south-westerly waves with a long fetch attack the base of the cliffs.
**What was at risk:** homes, roads, shops and the harbour (the Cobb), and the tourism economy.
**Tourism and heritage:** fossils, the Cobb and the beach attract many visitors.
**Environmental value:** the area is protected for its geology and wildlife (SSSI, Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty).
**Social impacts:** the threat of landslides made residents worried and reduced property values.
**Economic reasons:** the cost of damage from landslides outweighed the cost of protection, so a scheme was justified.
core.h: Case study: Lyme Regis, Dorset: reasons for management
core.p: Lyme Regis is a small seaside town on the **Jurassic Coast**, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, in Dorset. The cliffs around the town are made of weak clays, shales and limestone, including Blue Lias and Black Ven Marl, which are easily saturated by rain and by groundwater. This makes them very unstable and landslides and cliff slumping have happened regularly. The town's coast is also attacked by waves from the south-west which undercut the base of the cliffs. Over the years, landslides and erosion threatened homes, roads and the seafront and the town's tourism economy. The town depends on tourism and fossil hunting (it is where Mary Anning found famous fossils), so protecting the town and its beach was important to the local economy.

bullets: **Hard engineering:** sea wall and rock armour at the foot of the cliffs to stop undercutting.
**Slope stabilisation:** drains to remove groundwater, soil nailing and regrading to hold the slope.
**Soft engineering:** beach replenishment to restore a beach that protects the wall.
**Phased approach:** several phases over many years, each dealing with a different section of the coast.
**Funding:** public money (central government and local council), because of the benefit to the town.
**Aim:** protect properties and the economy and make the cliffs safer, while keeping tourism.
**Monitoring:** after the scheme, the cliffs and the beach are monitored to see whether it works.
**Check your own notes:** your teacher may use a different example (for example Holderness, Medmerry, Happisburgh or the Norfolk coast); the structure of your answer is the same.
core.h: Case study: Lyme Regis: the management strategy
core.p: Management in Lyme Regis was carried out in several **phases** over a number of years, the final one (Phase IV, the Eastern cliffs) being completed in about 2015 at a cost of roughly £20 million. It used a **combination of hard and soft** methods to deal with both wave erosion and landslides. At the base of the cliffs, **sea walls and rock armour** protect the toe from the waves. On the slopes, **drains** reduce the water in the cliff, **soil nails** and anchors hold the soil together, and **vegetation** helps bind the surface. A **new beach** created by beach replenishment widens the shore, helps absorb waves and supports tourism. The scheme was funded by the government (through Defra and the Environment Agency) and the local council.

bullets: **Positive economic effects:** protects homes and businesses; tourism continues; confidence for investment.
**Positive social effects:** residents feel safer; roads and paths remain open.
**Positive environmental effects:** a stable slope and a beach restored; planted vegetation.
**Negative effects:** very high cost; disruption during construction; loss of natural look.
**Conflicts:** geologists and fossil collectors versus residents; taxpayers versus beneficiaries; conservation versus development.
**Sustainability:** defences need maintenance and may not last if sea level rises faster than expected.
**Effects elsewhere:** reducing erosion in one place may reduce sediment for beaches along the coast.
**Judgement:** most people would say the scheme was successful in protecting the town, but at a high cost and with trade-offs.
core.p: A scheme has both **positive and negative effects** and can create **conflicts** between groups. At Lyme Regis the scheme made the town safer and more secure, which protected homes and the tourist economy, increased confidence in the town and made the beach more attractive. The cliffs are more stable, so landslide risk was reduced. However, hard defences and works have a **high cost**, and construction caused noise, disruption and the closure of some areas during building. Stabilising the cliffs can **cover fossil-bearing rocks**, which upsets fossil hunters and geologists who want natural erosion to expose new fossils. Some people do not like the appearance of the defences and loss of the natural landscape of a World Heritage Site. There may also be effects on other parts of the coast if sediment supply is reduced.

bullets: **Describe** a strategy: say what it is and how it works, then name one advantage and one disadvantage.
**Explain** why a strategy is used: link the problem (erosion, flooding) to the way the method helps.
**Assess/evaluate:** give advantages and disadvantages, weigh them, then conclude 'this is best because...'.
Use **named examples** with specific details (names, years, costs) to reach the top level.
In a **case study** answer, structure as reasons, strategy, effects (positive and negative), conflicts.
**Cost-benefit** answers: compare the value of what is protected with the cost, and give a ratio if data is given.
Always mention who **gains and loses** (stakeholders).
Practise drawing **annotated diagrams** of a sea wall, groynes and managed realignment.
core.p: Management questions often ask you to **assess** or **evaluate** a strategy or case study, usually for 6 or 9 marks (including SPaG marks in the larger questions). A good answer gives reasons, uses **named detail**, shows both sides, and reaches a **justified conclusion**. Use a structure such as point, evidence, explanation, evaluation (PEEL). For a data-response question, quote figures from the resource, such as costs per metre. Use the key terms precisely: hard engineering, soft engineering, sustainable, managed retreat, cost-benefit.

exam: **Describe a strategy** (2 to 3 marks): name it, say what it is made of, say how it works (reflects, absorbs, traps, adds sand).
**Explain how groynes work** (4 marks): they interrupt longshore drift, so sediment is deposited on the updrift side, the beach builds up, and the wider beach absorbs wave energy to protect the land.
**Advantages and disadvantages:** one developed point (point plus reason) is worth 2 marks; use 'this means', 'so', 'because'.
**Assess/evaluate (6 marks):** a balanced argument with both sides, a named example, and a final judgement.
**Case study structure:** reasons, strategy, effects (positive and negative), conflicts; use specific place names, costs and dates.
**Cost-benefit:** if given values, divide benefit by cost and say what it means (ratio above 1 = worth doing).
**Compare** hard and soft engineering: use comparative words such as 'whereas', 'in contrast', 'both'.
**Resource questions:** quote evidence (figures, labels) from the figure and link to the strategy.
**Sustainability:** say whether it meets needs without damaging future generations; link to cost and the environment.
**Conclusion:** state which approach is best for the place given the value of what is at risk.
**Use SPaG carefully** in extended answers: clear paragraphs and correct geographical terms.
Manage time: about one minute per mark.

mistakes.r: It is effective but costly and can increase erosion elsewhere; evaluate for the place.
mistakes.w: Hard engineering is always better because it lasts longer.

mistakes.r: Groynes trap sand on the updrift side but starve beaches downdrift, increasing erosion there.
mistakes.w: Groynes stop erosion everywhere on the coast.

mistakes.r: It is usually cheaper but needs repeated spending (e.g. nourishment) and management.
It is a planned policy that moves defences inland and creates natural defences such as salt marsh.
mistakes.w: Managed retreat means giving up the coast.

mistakes.r: Include reasons, named strategies, effects, and conflicts with place names and details.
mistakes.w: A case study answer just says 'a sea wall was built'.

mistakes.r: Curved sea walls reflect wave energy; rock armour absorbs it.
The sea removes the material, so it has to be repeated.
Cheaper than a wall but expensive to transport and place, and it can look unattractive.
mistakes.w: Rock armour is cheap because it is just rocks.

summary: You must know how hard engineering, soft engineering and managed retreat protect the coast, with the advantages, disadvantages and costs of each, and use a UK case study of a coastal management scheme (reasons, strategy, effects and conflicts). It matters because evaluation of management gives the high-mark questions in Paper 1.

terms.d: Building artificial structures to control natural processes and protect the coast.
Managing the coast by working with natural processes, such as adding sand or planting dunes.
A concrete or stone barrier, often with a curved face, built at the back of a beach to reflect wave energy.
Large boulders piled at the foot of a cliff or wall to absorb wave energy.
A timber or rock barrier built at right angles to the beach to trap sediment moved by longshore drift.
A wire cage filled with rocks, used to support cliffs or the base of slopes.
Adding sand or shingle to a beach to make it wider and higher.
Protecting and rebuilding sand dunes by fencing and planting marram grass.
Allowing the sea to flood or erode areas of land in a controlled way, usually with defences moved inland.
Another name for managed retreat; moving the line of defence landward.
A plan that sets a policy for each section of coast: hold the line, advance the line, managed realignment or no active intervention.
Comparing the cost of a scheme with the value of the land and property it would protect.
Meeting the needs of people today without damaging the environment or the ability of future generations to meet their needs.
Updrift is where sediment comes from along the coast; downdrift is where it moves to.
The fall in value of property in areas where defences will not be maintained.
A person or group affected by or with an interest in a decision.
A coastal wetland of mud and salt-tolerant plants that absorbs wave energy.

worked.ans: Groynes are barriers built at right angles to the beach, which interrupt longshore drift (1). Sand and shingle moving along the coast are trapped against the groyne and deposited on the updrift side (1). This builds up a wider, higher beach (1), which absorbs wave energy, so less energy reaches the cliff or defences and erosion is reduced (1). (4 marks)
worked.q: Explain how groynes reduce coastal erosion. (4 marks)
steps: Beach builds up on updrift side.
Wider beach absorbs wave energy, protecting the land.

worked.ans: Benefit = £18 million (1). Ratio = 18 ÷ 2.4 = 7.5 (1). Since the ratio is above 1 the scheme is good value for money, because the value of the property protected is 7.5 times the cost (1). (Illustrative figures.) (3 marks)
worked.q: A beach nourishment scheme costs £2.4 million and protects 120 properties each worth £150 000. Calculate the cost-benefit ratio and say what it shows. (3 marks)
steps: A ratio above 1 means the benefit is greater than the cost.

worked.ans: At Lyme Regis in Dorset the weak clays and shales of the cliffs were unstable and waves undercut the base, which threatened homes, roads and the tourism economy (1). The scheme used a combination of strategies, including rock armour and sea wall at the base, drainage and soil nailing to stabilise the slope, and beach replenishment (2). It was a success because it made the town safer, protected the economy and maintained a beach for tourists (1). However, the scheme cost around £20 million, caused disruption during construction, and covered natural cliffs where fossil hunters and geologists wanted erosion to expose new fossils, so there was conflict between groups (1). Overall it was largely successful for the residents because the benefits to the town were greater than the costs, but it is not a permanent solution because defences will need maintaining as sea level rises (1). (6 marks)
